lessonActivities.title: What Is a Compound Adjective? 🎯
lessonActivities.content: Imagine describing a film as 'spine-chilling' or a performance as 'record-breaking' — these are **compound adjectives**! 🎬📚**Compound adjective** = an adjective made up of two or more words joined together to describe a noun.*Example: It was a **badly-lit** hall. | We saw a **man-eating** alligator.*Why does hyphenation matter? Look at the difference:**A man eating alligator** → a man who is eating an alligator 🤔**A man-eating alligator** → an alligator that eats men! 😱The hyphen changes meaning. Without it, ambiguity sneaks in.**Key rule:** When the compound comes **before** a noun, hyphenate it. When it comes **after** a verb, the hyphen is often dropped.*Fun fact: English creates new compound adjectives constantly — 'user-friendly' was invented in the 1970s! 💡*
examples: After verb (no hyphen): The author is **well known**.
functions: Describing nouns with more precision than single adjectives
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 **Quick Rule:** Compound before a noun = hyphen. Compound after 'is/was/seems' = usually no hyphen. *A well-known actor* vs *The actor is well known.*

lessonActivities.title: Adjective + Noun Compounds 🚀
lessonActivities.content: Now let's level up! 🎮 The first big compound type: **Adjective + Noun**.**Pattern:** [adjective] + [noun] → compound adjective*Examples:*full-length (full + length): *a full-length portrait*blue-collar (blue + collar): *blue-collar workers*last-minute (last + minute): *a last-minute decision*deep-sea (deep + sea): *deep-sea diving*short-term / long-term: *a short-term contract***Notice:** The compound works as one unit to describe the main noun — 'full-length portrait' means a portrait showing the full body, not a long portrait!*Fun fact: 'Blue-collar' originated in the USA in the 1920s, referring to workers who wore blue work uniforms! 🌟*
examples: Adjective + Noun: **a last-minute** decision (the decision happened at the last minute)
Adjective + Noun: **a short-term** contract (a contract for a short term)
functions: Compressing two-word descriptions into precise pre-noun modifiers
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 **Memory trick:** If [adjective] + [noun] together describe how the main noun IS or what it IS FOR, join them with a hyphen before the noun.

lessonActivities.title: Noun + Adjective Compounds 🌟
lessonActivities.content: Time to explore another way! ✨ **Noun + Adjective** compounds flip the order — the noun comes first.**Pattern:** [noun] + [adjective] → compound adjective*Examples:*smoke-free (smoke + free): *a smoke-free area*ice-cold (ice + cold): *ice-cold drinks*world-famous (world + famous): *a world-famous actor*user-friendly (user + friendly): *a user-friendly website*water-resistant (water + resistant): *a water-resistant watch***Compare:****Adjective + Noun**: full-length, last-minute**Noun + Adjective**: ice-cold, world-famous*The noun in these compounds acts as a qualifier showing 'in relation to what' the adjective applies.*Fun fact: 'User-friendly' is now used metaphorically for anything easy to use — even people can be 'user-friendly'! 🎨*
examples: Noun + Adjective: **ice-cold** drinks (as cold as ice)
functions: Expressing qualities relative to a reference noun
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 **Decision point:** If the noun tells you what the adjective relates to (free from *smoke*, cold as *ice*), it's likely a Noun + Adjective compound.

lessonActivities.title: Compounds with Participles ⚡
lessonActivities.content: Here's where it gets interesting! 🤔 Many compound adjectives use **present participle (-ing)** or **past participle (-ed/-en)** as the second element.**Adjective + Present Participle:**good-looking, far-reaching, quick-thinking, long-lasting, easy-going*Examples: a good-looking actor | a far-reaching decision***Noun + Present Participle:**coal-mining, eye-opening, mouth-watering, time-saving, record-breaking*Examples: a record-breaking performance | mouth-watering food***Noun + Past Participle:**sun-dried, middle-aged, wind-powered, tree-lined, shop-soiled*Examples: sun-dried tomatoes | a tree-lined avenue***Adjective + Past Participle:**old-fashioned, narrow-minded, cold-blooded, level-headed*Examples: an old-fashioned style | a level-headed person**Common mistake:** ❌ 'good looking' (before noun) → ✅ 'a good-looking person' 🎯*
functions: Forming compounds using -ing and -ed/-en participle forms
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 **Pro tip:** If you see a compound adjective ending in -ing or -ed/-en, identify whether the first part is an adjective, noun, or adverb — that tells you its type.

lessonActivities.title: Adverb + Past Participle Compounds 🎯
lessonActivities.content: Ready for the next level? 🚀 **Adverb + Past Participle** compounds are incredibly common in formal and professional English.**Pattern:** [adverb] + [past participle] → compound*Examples:*deeply-rooted: *These people hold deeply-rooted beliefs.*well-prepared: *The leader gave a well-prepared speech.*highly-respected: *a highly-respected scholar*badly-behaved: *a group of badly-behaved children*densely-populated: *a densely-populated city***These are especially common in academic writing and journalism.**Other common forms:** widely-recognized, poorly-paid, brightly-lit, tightly-wound, long-forgotten, much-needed, long-awaited*Fun fact: 'Well-prepared' can describe both a speech AND a meal — context makes the meaning clear! ⚙️*
examples: At a specific time: **a well-prepared** presentation
functions: Using adverb+participle compounds in formal and academic contexts
Intensifying past participle descriptors with adverbs
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 **When to use:** Adverb + Past Participle compounds add precision to descriptions — especially useful in essays, reports, and professional writing.

lessonActivities.title: Number + Noun Compounds ❓
lessonActivities.content: Let's master the number compounds! 🔢 **Number + Noun (singular)** compounds are extremely common in everyday English.**Key rule:** The noun in a number+noun compound is always **singular**, even if the number is greater than one!*Examples:*ten-minute break (NOT ten-minutes break ❌)*five-day week (NOT five-days week ❌)*twenty-storey building*three-hour film*five-star hotel***Pattern:** [number] + [singular noun] — always hyphenated before the noun.*More examples:*a two-way street | a ten-page document | a three-week holiday | a six-foot ladder*They answer the question 'what kind of ___?' and measure duration, size, or quantity.*Fun fact: 'Five-star' originally described hotel ratings — now it's used for anything excellent! 💬*
examples: Negative (wrong): a ❌ five-**days** trip → ✅ a **five-day** trip
Yes/No: Was it a **ten-minute** break? Yes, it was a ten-minute break.
functions: Forming number+noun compound adjectives with singular nouns
Describing duration, size, measurement, and quantity
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 **Remember:** Number + Noun compounds ALWAYS use singular nouns. 'A five-day week', 'a three-hour film' — never 'five-days' or 'three-hours'.

lessonActivities.title: Idiomatic Phrase Compounds 🕐
lessonActivities.content: Here's a crucial rule! ⚠️ Some compound adjectives are built from entire **idiomatic phrases**, usually hyphenated across multiple words.**Common idiomatic compounds:**middle-of-the-road: *a middle-of-the-road entertainer* (neither extreme)*off-the-rack: *off-the-rack suits* (ready-made, not tailored)*over-the-counter: *over-the-counter medicine* (no prescription needed)*once-in-a-lifetime: *a once-in-a-lifetime experience* (happens only once)*one-of-a-kind: *a one-of-a-kind design* (completely unique)*all-too-common: *an all-too-common mistake* (unfortunately frequent)**⚠️ These are always hyphenated** when they precede the noun — every word in the phrase gets a hyphen.*Fun fact: 'Over-the-counter' is now used globally, but originally referred to medicine sold directly across a pharmacy counter! 🌍*
examples: With 'off-the-rack': He wore an **off-the-rack** suit to the interview.
functions: Recognising and using multi-word idiomatic compound adjectives
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 **Never forget:** Multi-word phrase compounds are hyphenated throughout when before a noun: once**-**in**-**a**-**lifetime experience. Every word joins the chain!

lessonActivities.title: Compound Adjective Mastery 🏆
lessonActivities.content: You've come so far! 🌟 Let's tackle the **advanced nuances** that separate good from great.**Special Case 1: Hyphen position matters**'A little-used road' (a road that is little used) vs 'A little used road' (ambiguous — a small, used road?). The hyphen prevents misreading.**Special Case 2: Compound adjectives in predicative position**Before noun: *a well-known fact* → After verb: *The fact is **well known*** (no hyphen in most style guides).**Sophisticated Usage:**[Formal]: *a densely-populated, resource-limited coastal region* — compounds stack in formal writing.**[Informal]**: 'That's a mind-blowing idea!' (spoken with emphasis)**Mastery checklist:** ✅ Hyphen before noun ✅ No hyphen after verb ✅ Singular noun in number compounds ✅ Full-phrase hyphenation for idiomatic forms*Fun fact: 'Bittersweet' started as a compound adjective and is now treated as a single word — language evolves! 🎓*
examples: Ambiguity resolved: **a man-eating** shark (not 'a man eating shark')
Position shift: **a well-prepared** meal → The meal was **well prepared**.
functions: Applying hyphenation rules for pre-noun vs predicative positions
Using stacked compound adjectives in formal writing
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 **Master level:** Before noun = hyphen. After verb = no hyphen (usually). Always check: does removing the hyphen create ambiguity? If yes, keep it!

writingActivities.question: Describe your ideal home or workspace using at least 4 compound adjectives. Include: one adjective+noun compound, one noun+adjective compound, and one number+noun compound.
writingActivities.hint: Start with 'My ideal [home/workspace] would have a ___.' Examples: energy-efficient windows, a smoke-free environment, a ten-minute commute. Hyphenate all compounds that appear before a noun!
sentenceStarters: My ideal ___ would be ___ [compound adj] and ___.
I would want a ___ [number-noun] ___ and a ___ [noun-adj] ___.

writingActivities.question: Write a short review of a film, restaurant, or product using at least 5 compound adjectives from different types: adjective+participle, noun+participle, and adverb+participle. Show correct hyphenation.
writingActivities.hint: Remember: well-prepared, mouth-watering, record-breaking, highly-rated, long-awaited are all examples. Hyphenate before the noun, drop the hyphen after 'is/was'. Example: *The food was mouth-watering. It was a well-prepared, highly-rated experience.*
sentenceStarters: The ___ was [compound adj]. It was a ___ [compound adj] ___.

writingActivities.question: Write a paragraph about an extraordinary travel experience (real or imaginary) using at least 6 compound adjectives. Include: two idiomatic phrase compounds, one number+noun compound, and one adverb+participle compound. Pay attention to hyphenation throughout.
writingActivities.hint: This requires the most advanced compound types. Example: *It was a once-in-a-lifetime, three-week journey through a densely-populated, world-famous region. Each moment was an eye-opening, all-too-rare experience.*
sentenceStarters: It was a once-in-a-lifetime ___ that felt ___.
Although the ___ [number-noun] trip was ___ [compound adj], it was a ___ [idiomatic] experience.

gameActivities.question: Choose the correct compound adjective type for this sentence:
gameActivities.sentence: They signed a ____ contract with the company.
gameActivities.hint: Adjective + Noun compound before a noun — always hyphenate.

gameActivities.question: Which form is correct when the compound comes AFTER the verb?
gameActivities.hint: After a linking verb (is/was), compound adjectives are usually written WITHOUT a hyphen.

gameActivities.question: Which number+noun compound is correctly formed?
gameActivities.hint: Number + Noun compounds use singular nouns and a hyphen.

gameActivities.question: Choose the correct compound adjective for this sentence:
gameActivities.hint: Noun + Present Participle compound before a noun — hyphenate.

gameActivities.question: Which compound correctly describes a product with no added sugar?
gameActivities.hint: Noun + Adjective compound — hyphenate before the noun.

gameActivities.question: Pick the correct adverb+participle compound:
gameActivities.sentence: The region is home to a ____ population.
gameActivities.hint: Adverb + Past Participle — hyphenate before the noun it modifies.

gameActivities.question: Which idiomatic compound adjective means 'neither extreme — average and safe'?
gameActivities.hint: Idiomatic phrase compounds: every word in the phrase gets a hyphen before the noun.

gameActivities.question: Which sentence is correctly written with the compound adjective in predicative position?
gameActivities.hint: Before the noun = hyphen. After the verb = no hyphen.

gameActivities.question: Advanced: Which sentence uses ambiguity-resolving hyphenation correctly?
gameActivities.sentence: Choose the option where the hyphen prevents misreading:
options: We saw a man eating alligator.
gameActivities.hint: Without the hyphen, 'man eating alligator' could mean a man who is eating an alligator!

gameActivities.question: What type of compound adjective is 'old-fashioned'?
gameActivities.hint: 'Old' is an adjective, 'fashioned' is a past participle.

quizActivities.question: Why are compound adjectives hyphenated before a noun?
quizActivities.sentence: She wore a **well-chosen** dress. / The dress was **well chosen**.
options: To make the word look longer
To prevent ambiguity and show the words work together as one modifier
To separate the adjective from the noun
quizActivities.correctAnswer: To prevent ambiguity and show the words work together as one modifier
quizActivities.hint: Think about how 'man eating alligator' vs 'man-eating alligator' have different meanings.
quizActivities.explanation: Hyphens in compound adjectives signal that the words function as a single unit to modify the noun. This prevents misreading: 'a man-eating alligator' is an alligator that eats men, while 'a man eating alligator' reads as a man who is eating an alligator. When the compound comes after the verb, the hyphen is usually dropped as context makes the meaning clear.

quizActivities.question: Which of these is an Adjective + Noun compound?
quizActivities.hint: Adjective + Noun: the first word is an adjective (last) and the second is a noun (minute).
quizActivities.explanation: 'Last-minute' = Adjective (last) + Noun (minute). 'Record-breaking' = Noun + Present Participle. 'Well-prepared' = Adverb + Past Participle. 'Sun-dried' = Noun + Past Participle. Identifying compound types helps learners predict and form new compounds correctly.

quizActivities.question: In number + noun compounds, what form must the noun take?
quizActivities.hint: The noun in a number+noun compound is ALWAYS singular.
quizActivities.explanation: In number + noun compound adjectives, the noun is always singular regardless of the number: 'a five-star hotel', 'a ten-minute break', 'a three-week holiday'. Adding a plural -s ('five-stars', 'ten-minutes') is a very common error — the compound acts as a single descriptive unit, not a literal count.

quizActivities.question: Which option correctly uses a compound adjective in the predicative (after-verb) position?
options: The actor is well-known for his roles.
The well-known actor received an award.
The actor is wellknown for his roles.
The actor is well knowing for his roles.
quizActivities.correctAnswer: The actor is well-known for his roles.
quizActivities.hint: In predicative position, some style guides drop the hyphen, but many keep it — both 'well known' and 'well-known' after a verb are acceptable.
quizActivities.explanation: In predicative position (after a verb), compound adjectives are commonly written without a hyphen ('well known') in many style guides, though 'well-known' is also accepted. 'The well-known actor' (attributive, before noun) is definitively hyphenated. 'Wellknown' as one word is never correct, and 'well knowing' changes the meaning entirely.

quizActivities.question: What makes 'once-in-a-lifetime' an idiomatic compound adjective?
options: It is formed from an entire idiomatic phrase, all hyphenated before the noun
It cannot be used after a verb
quizActivities.correctAnswer: It is formed from an entire idiomatic phrase, all hyphenated before the noun
quizActivities.hint: Idiomatic compounds can be whole phrases — every word in the phrase gets a hyphen.
quizActivities.explanation: 'Once-in-a-lifetime' is an idiomatic phrase compound: the entire expression 'once in a lifetime' becomes a compound adjective when placed before a noun, with hyphens connecting every word. This distinguishes it from number+noun or adjective+participle types. Other examples: 'middle-of-the-road', 'off-the-rack', 'over-the-counter'.

quizActivities.question: Which compound type is 'mouth-watering'?
quizActivities.hint: 'Mouth' is a noun; 'watering' is a present participle (-ing form).
quizActivities.explanation: 'Mouth-watering' = Noun (mouth) + Present Participle (watering). This type includes: coal-mining, eye-opening, time-saving, record-breaking. The noun specifies the subject or context of the participle action.

quizActivities.question: Which adverb + past participle compound adjective is correctly formed?
quizActivities.sentence: Choose the correct option for this sentence: 'The city is ____.'
quizActivities.hint: After a verb (predicative position), the hyphen is typically dropped.
quizActivities.explanation: 'Densely populated' is correct in predicative position (after 'is'). In attributive position it would be 'a densely-populated city'. 'Dense-populated' incorrectly uses an adjective instead of the adverb 'densely'. 'Densely-populate' uses the wrong verb form.

quizActivities.question: What type of compound adjective is 'narrow-minded'?
quizActivities.sentence: My grandfather was a narrow-minded man.
quizActivities.hint: 'Narrow' is an adjective; 'minded' comes from the past participle of 'to mind'.
quizActivities.explanation: 'Narrow-minded' = Adjective (narrow) + Past Participle (minded). Other examples of this type: old-fashioned, cold-blooded, level-headed, red-haired, absent-minded, high-pitched. The adjective describes the quality of the participle.

quizActivities.question: Which sentence INCORRECTLY uses a compound adjective?
options: He wore a blue-collars worker's uniform.
quizActivities.correctAnswer: He wore a blue-collars worker's uniform.
quizActivities.hint: Look for the error in how the compound adjective is formed.
quizActivities.explanation: 'Blue-collars' is wrong — compound adjectives do not take plural -s on either component. The correct form is 'blue-collar'. All other options are correct: 'user-friendly' (Noun+Adjective), 'world-famous' (Noun+Adjective), 'three-week' (Number+Noun, singular noun).

quizActivities.question: Which of these is an example of an 'Adjective + Present Participle' compound?
quizActivities.sentence: Identify the compound type from the options:
quizActivities.hint: 'Easy' is an adjective; 'going' is a present participle.
quizActivities.explanation: 'Easy-going' = Adjective (easy) + Present Participle (going). Other Adjective + Present Participle examples: good-looking, far-reaching, quick-thinking, long-lasting, fast-talking. 'Record-breaking' is Noun + Present Participle. 'Sun-dried' is Noun + Past Participle. 'World-famous' is Noun + Adjective.
